newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW - LOW FINNISH YIELDS PRESSURE PENSIONS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - LOW FINNISH YIELDS PRESSURE PENSIONS.

text.p: The recent fall in interest rates puts pressure on pension contributions to rise, Kari Puro, CEO of pension insurer Ilmarinen said on Friday.

In funding pensions, the ratio between contributions and investment return is determined by a minimum required rate of return set by the ministy of social and health affairs and next year, this will have to be lowered from the current 6.00 percent due to the fall in interest rates, Puro said.
"Sometime next year this level can't be supported anymore," Puro told Reuters in an interview.
"But exactly when and by how much, I can't say yet," he added.

Of the six percent return required to fund the system, five percentage points worth of revenue is added to cover future liabilities and one percentage point is paid to today's pensioners, so if the rate were lowered to 5.00 percent, current contributions would rise correspondingly.
"That would mean a 1.2 percentage point increase in the rate of contributions," Puro said, adding that this would by law be split equally between employers and employees.

So while the government on one side is cutting income taxes next year by about two percentage points, the pension system may up the tax wedge on the other side by 1.2 percentage points, about half of which would be paid by wage-earners.
The total annual wage sum in Finland is about 240 billion markka. A 0.6 percentage point increase in taxpayers pension contribution would reduce disposable income by 1.4 billion markka.

Although the required rate of return is set by the ministry at the pension funds' requests, it follows an agreement between the pension insurers and the labour market organisations, which always oppose lowering it since that ups contributions, Puro said.
However, the protests become meaningless if returns on near risk-free financial instruments do not meet the requirement.
Necessity will ultimately rule since, by law, insurers must meet the minimun rate requirement.
"Say the (labour market) organisations what they will, the companies must apply for a rate they can fulfil," he said.
On the other hand, pension insurers can't boost returns by choosing riskier instruments since their working capital provides an insufficient buffer against more volatile asset values, Puro said.

The system was created in the 1960s when real interest rates were about or below zero and the bulk of pension funds were invested in fully collateralised loans back to the companies at set interest rates. In that environment no buffers were needed.
Puro chairs a committe appointed by the ministry of social and health affairs last year to find ways to adapt the system to the new environment where risk is an ever-present element in investment.
This is not easy, Puro said.

"The problems are that lending back is not competitive with interest rates, and with the required full collateralisation, government bonds are now the only possible instrument ... and we lack working capital to invest in shares," he said.
He noted that the only sources for more working capital as a buffer for risks are in the system itself -- the funds and the contributors.
Unless, of course, investment income could rise, but this would again increase risks which would require more capital which would require higher investment income which would ...
Puro said that any hopes for a massive flow of funds to the stockmarket from pension funds are in vain.
"In the best possible outcome, if we could find a way to increase working capital ... the amount of shares which is currently six billion to seven billion markka could double in ten years," he said.
Compared to the total market capitalisation of shares on the Helsinki Stock Exchange -- 242.9 billion markka at end-August -- that would be marginal, he said.
